So, yeah, the hologram itself is not damaged. What's damaged is the glass to which it was laminated, and it has to be either delaminated or used as a master to shoot another hologram of itself. And you can do contact printing. See if that helps. On a tripod. Just tilt it. You should be inside the frame. There's the aperture. There you go. So, this is Escher falling, the original master. It's done with a pulsed laser in Las Vegas in 2006 or 2007. I can't remember. And it's a cut-up. It's a cut-up of M.C. Escher's Another World. And it has cracks in it right now because the glass to which it was laminated was cracked. But the hologram is not... It's not damaged. Now, that's pretty nice. You can see that it's got levels. It's actually four feet deep. And I could get inside of it a little bit now. Let's see if I can get a... There we go. Oh, yeah. This is very nice. You can see the cracks. They're unavoidable, really. If I get inside the cracks, you won't see the other part of this image. So this is really beautifully spatial. And I've made rainbow holograms from that, which are illuminated by white light and were used in other creations. A page out of Escher has three rainbow holograms. And I've been experimenting with different interpretations of this. But by itself, this hologram could be illuminated by any color and could be converted to rainbow or achromat, which is black and white. Holographically. But there hasn't been the time or the money to do that. It just makes me think of... I would like to see that animated. It makes me think of a collage. Yeah. You can have that in a pop-up book, right? Oh, you could. I have a pop-up book of that piece. But the pop-up is very... Actually, it's a good idea to just pop it up. Right after we film this. So that we have a reference of how other people saw this. It's the only Escher work you put in, huh? Yeah.
